# Proof

**Conventions.** $X$ is a (smooth) $1$-manifold, possibly with boundary; in particular $X$ is Hausdorff and every point $x\in X$ has an open neighbourhood $V$ with a homeomorphism $\varphi:V\to\varphi(V)$ onto an open subset of $\R$ or of $H=[0,\infty)$. Only these topological facts are used. "$L$ is diffeomorphic to an open interval" gives in particular a homeomorphism $(a,b)\to L$ ($-\infty\le a<b\le\infty$, $L$ with the subspace topology); composing with a homeomorphism $(0,1)\to(a,b)$ we obtain a continuous injective map $f:(0,1)\to X$ with $f((0,1))=L$.

**Lemma.** Let $I\subseteq\R$ be an interval and $g:I\to\R$ continuous and injective. Then $g$ is strictly monotone. Consequently, if $I=(0,\beta)$ and $g$ is bounded, then $m=\lim_{t\to0^+}g(t)$ exists; similarly at a right endpoint.

*Proof.* Suppose $g$ is not strictly decreasing, so there are $x<y$ in $I$ with $g(x)<g(y)$. Let $u<w$ be arbitrary in $I$. For $\lambda\in[0,1]$ put $a(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)u+\lambda x$ and $b(\lambda)=(1-\lambda)w+\lambda y$. These lie in $I$ (convexity), and $a(\lambda)<b(\lambda)$. The function $G(\lambda)=g(b(\lambda))-g(a(\lambda))$ is continuous on $[0,1]$ and never $0$ by injectivity, and $G(1)=g(y)-g(x)>0$. By the intermediate value theorem $G(0)=g(w)-g(u)>0$. Hence $g$ is strictly increasing. So $g$ is either strictly decreasing or strictly increasing. A bounded monotone function on $(0,\beta)$ has a limit as $t\to0^+$ (the infimum or the supremum of its values), and the same holds at a right endpoint. $\square$

**Main claim.** For every $p\in\cl(L)\setminus L$ there is $e\in\{0,1\}$ with $\lim_{t\to e}f(t)=p$.

Granting this, the claim follows: in the Hausdorff space $X$ a limit is unique, so the rule $p\mapsto e$ is an injective map $\cl(L)\setminus L\to\{0,1\}$, and hence $\cl(L)\setminus L$ has at most two points.

*Proof of the main claim.* Fix $p\in\cl(L)\setminus L$ and a chart $\varphi:V\to\varphi(V)$ with $p\in V$; put $c=\varphi(p)$.

*Choice of $r$.* If $\varphi(V)$ is open in $\R$, or $\varphi(V)\subseteq H$ with $c>0$ ("interior case"), choose $r>0$ with $K:=[c-r,c+r]\subseteq\varphi(V)$ and set $J=(c-r,c+r)$. If $\varphi(V)\subseteq H$ and $c=0$ ("boundary case"), choose $r>0$ with $K:=[0,r]\subseteq\varphi(V)$ and set $J=[0,r)=H\cap(-r,r)$. In both cases $J$ is open in $\varphi(V)$, so $W:=\varphi^{-1}(J)$ is open in $V$ and hence in $X$, and $p\in W$. The set $\varphi^{-1}(K)$ is compact, hence closed in the Hausdorff space $X$, and contains $W$; thus $\overline W\subseteq\varphi^{-1}(K)\subseteq V$ and
$$\overline W\setminus W\subseteq \varphi^{-1}(K\setminus J),\qquad K\setminus J=\begin{cases}\{c-r,c+r\}&\text{interior case},\\ \{r\}&\text{boundary case.}\end{cases}$$

Let $O=f^{-1}(W)$, an open subset of $(0,1)$, and $g=\varphi\circ f|_O:O\to J$, continuous and injective. Since $p\notin L$, $g(t)\neq c$ for all $t\in O$.

*Step 1: every connected component $(\alpha,\beta)$ of $O$ has $\alpha=0$ or $\beta=1$.* Suppose $0<\alpha<\beta<1$. The endpoints of a component of an open subset of $(0,1)$ lying in $(0,1)$ are not in $O$, so $f(\alpha),f(\beta)\notin W$. But $f(\alpha)=\lim_{t\to\alpha^+}f(t)$ with $f(t)\in W$ for $t\in(\alpha,\beta)$, so $f(\alpha)\in\overline W\setminus W$; likewise $f(\beta)$. Hence $f([\alpha,\beta])\subseteq\overline W\subseteq V$ and $h=\varphi\circ f|_{[\alpha,\beta]}$ is continuous and injective, with $h(\alpha),h(\beta)\in K\setminus J$ and $h(\alpha)\ne h(\beta)$. In the boundary case $K\setminus J$ has one element: contradiction. In the interior case $\{h(\alpha),h(\beta)\}=\{c-r,c+r\}$, so by the intermediate value theorem $h(s)=c$ for some $s\in(\alpha,\beta)$, i.e. $f(s)=p\in L$: contradiction.

*Step 2.* Distinct components are disjoint, so at most one component has left endpoint $0$ and at most one has right endpoint $1$. By Step 1, $O$ has at most two components.

*Step 3: a sequence.* For $n$ with $1/n<r$, the set $\varphi^{-1}(\varphi(V)\cap(c-1/n,c+1/n))$ is an open neighbourhood of $p$ in $X$ contained in $W$; as $p\in\cl(L)$ it contains a point $f(t_n)$, so $t_n\in O$ and $|g(t_n)-c|<1/n$. Thus $g(t_n)\to c$, and since $\varphi^{-1}$ is continuous, $f(t_n)=\varphi^{-1}(g(t_n))\to p$. By Step 2 and compactness of $[0,1]$, after passing to a subsequence all $t_n$ lie in a single component $C$ of $O$ and $t_n\to s\in[0,1]$.

*Step 4.* If $s\in(0,1)$, continuity gives $f(t_n)\to f(s)$; by uniqueness of limits $p=f(s)\in L$, a contradiction. So $s\in\{0,1\}$; say $s=0$ (the case $s=1$ is symmetric). Since $t_n\in C$ and $t_n\to0$, $C=(0,\beta)$. By the Lemma, $g|_C$ (bounded, with values in $J$) is strictly monotone and $m=\lim_{t\to0^+}g(t)$ exists; as $g(t_n)\to c$, $m=c$. Hence $g(t)\to c$ as $t\to0^+$, and $f(t)=\varphi^{-1}(g(t))\to\varphi^{-1}(c)=p$ as $t\to 0^+$ (for $t\in C$, which contains all small $t$). This proves the main claim with $e=0$. $\square$

Therefore $\cl(L)$ contains at most two points not in $L$. $\blacksquare$
